Note::tokenize_words¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note::tokenize_words() const -> TokenBatch
Note::tokenize_words(std::int64_t flags) const -> TokenBatch

What It Does¶

Tokenizes each text cell into word-like units.

This sits one step above raw delimiter splitting: instead of splitting on a single literal character or on whitespace only, tokenize_words() applies the library’s word tokenization behavior and returns a flattened token stream with case offsets.

Use this when punctuation and spacing are not enough to describe the token boundaries you want. It is the bridge between very light structural splitting and fuller NLP surfaces.

Parameters¶

flags

Optional tokenizer-behavior flags.

  • tokenize_words() Uses the library’s default word-tokenization policy.

  • tokenize_words(flags) Uses an explicit flag bitmask. Reach for this overload only when you already know the library-defined flag contract you want to opt into.

This page does not invent semantics for unnamed flag bits. When a future pass documents a specific flag family, it should do so with explicit flag names and verified examples rather than hand-waving about possible behaviors.

Returns¶

TokenBatch A flat word-token stream plus offsets() describing which tokens belong to each input cell.

Examples¶

Example 1. Tokenize mixed punctuation and newline text into words.

auto note = pluss::make_note({"One.\nTwo!", "A,b;c"});
auto out = note.tokenize_words();
std::cout << "tokenize_words tokens:";
for (std::int64_t i = 0; i < out.tokens().numel(); ++i) {
  std::cout << " [" << out.tokens().at(i) << "]";
}
std::cout << "\n";
std::cout << "tokenize_words offsets:";
for (std::int64_t off : out.offsets()) {
  std::cout << " " << off;
}
std::cout << "\n";

Output¶

tokenize_words tokens: [One] [Two] [A] [b] [c]
tokenize_words offsets: 0 2 5

Example 2. Normalize case first when you want lowercase word tokens directly.

auto note = pluss::make_note({"Ada LOVELACE", "Grace Hopper"});
auto lower = note.lower();
auto out = lower.tokenize_words();
std::cout << "tokenize_words_lower tokens:";
for (std::int64_t i = 0; i < out.tokens().numel(); ++i) {
  std::cout << " [" << out.tokens().at(i) << "]";
}
std::cout << "\n";
std::cout << "tokenize_words_lower offsets:";
for (std::int64_t off : out.offsets()) {
  std::cout << " " << off;
}
std::cout << "\n";

Output¶

tokenize_words_lower tokens: [ada] [lovelace] [grace] [hopper]
tokenize_words_lower offsets: 0 2 4

Example 3. Compare it mentally with split_whitespace() when you want a more word-like split but still need to see what the default tokenizer keeps intact.

auto note = pluss::make_note({"price=12.50, paid!", "ref:A-17"});
auto out = note.tokenize_words();
std::cout << "tokenize_words_punct tokens:";
for (std::int64_t i = 0; i < out.tokens().numel(); ++i) {
  std::cout << " [" << out.tokens().at(i) << "]";
}
std::cout << "\n";
std::cout << "tokenize_words_punct offsets:";
for (std::int64_t off : out.offsets()) {
  std::cout << " " << off;
}
std::cout << "\n";

Output¶

tokenize_words_punct tokens: [price] [12] [50] [paid] [ref] [A-17]
tokenize_words_punct offsets: 0 4 6

Notes¶

  • The current default behavior often strips obvious punctuation boundaries, but some compound fragments can remain intact, as A-17 does in the third example.

  • offsets() show that the first input cell contributed two words and the second contributed three.

  • If your use case is pure whitespace structure without word-token logic, split_whitespace is the more direct primitive.

See Also¶

  • Note::split_whitespace: simpler structural token splitting.

  • Note::regex_findall: extract only tokens that match a pattern.
